details:
**The Bald Soprano**
Ionesco's first play (1950), which he called an "anti-play," inspired by the empty dialogue of an English-language phrase book. An English couple, the Smiths, receive their friends the Martins, and their conversation decays into clichés and non-sequiturs. It opens with an "English clock" striking seventeen "English strokes," and it ends with the Martins repeating the Smiths' opening lines, showing the play's circularity.

**Rhinoceros and Berenger**
Ionesco's most famous play (1959), an allegory of conformity and the rise of fascism and Nazism in which the inhabitants of a small town turn one by one into rhinoceroses. The everyman Berenger is the only one who resists, and the play ends with his defiant cry, "I'm not capitulating!"

**Daisy, Dudard, Jean, and Mrs. Boeuf**
Characters in Rhinoceros who give in to the transformation. Berenger's friend Jean declares "Humanism is dead" as he turns into a rhinoceros before Berenger's eyes. Mrs. Boeuf leaps down a crushed staircase to join her husband after recognizing him as a rhinoceros, and the office colleagues Botard and Dudard also convert. Berenger's love Daisy is the last to leave him and join the herd.

**The Logician**
A character in Act I of Rhinoceros who delivers absurd syllogisms to the Old Gentleman, for example proving that because all cats die and Socrates died, Socrates must be a cat.

**The Chairs**
A 1952 play in which an Old Man and Old Woman on an island arrange more and more chairs for invisible guests, including an invisible Emperor, who have come to hear the Old Man's message to humanity. Once the Orator arrives to deliver it, the couple shout "Long live the Emperor!" and jump out the windows to their deaths.

**The deaf-mute Orator**
The professional speaker hired to deliver the Old Man's message at the end of The Chairs. After the couple's suicide he turns out to be deaf and mute, can only make guttural sounds, and writes a meaningless string of letters on a blackboard, including a garbled "ANGELFOOD," before leaving the stage to the empty chairs.

**Semiramis and "Then at last we arrived"**
In The Chairs, the Old Woman, whom her 95-year-old husband calls Semiramis, asks him to tell the same story he tells every night, which begins "Then at last we arrived" and concerns a journey to a Paris that he says vanished long ago. She consoles him that if he had wanted, he could have been "head president, head king, or even head doctor."

**The Martins' recognition scene**
In The Bald Soprano, Mr. and Mrs. Martin talk as strangers and slowly realize, through a string of coincidences (the same train, the same street and apartment, a daughter named Alice with one white eye and one red eye), that they must be husband and wife, and they embrace. The maid Mary then reveals that the two children's eyes are on opposite sides, so he is not Donald and she is not Elizabeth.

**Bobby Watson**
In The Bald Soprano, the Smiths discuss the death of Bobby Watson, and it turns out that his wife, and seemingly every member of his family, is also named Bobby Watson, making it impossible to tell who is who.

**The Fire Chief and the bald soprano**
The Fire Chief drops in on the Smiths and Martins looking for a fire to put out. He tells absurd anecdotes, such as one about a calf that ate ground glass and gave birth to a cow, and Mary the maid, who claims to be Sherlock Holmes, recites a poem called "The Fire" in his honor. As he leaves he asks about "the bald soprano," and Mrs. Smith answers that she "always wears her hair in the same style." The title figure never appears.

**The Lesson**
A 1951 one-act play in which a Professor tutors a young Pupil. She can multiply huge numbers only because she has memorized every possible product but cannot subtract; she develops a toothache, and the increasingly violent Professor stabs her with an (often imaginary) knife. The Maid then brings in the next Pupil. The Lesson and The Bald Soprano have run together at the Théâtre de la Huchette in Paris continuously since 1957.

**The Killer**
A play of the Berenger cycle in which Berenger visits a "radiant city" plagued by a murderer who lures victims to a pool by offering to show them "a picture of the colonel" and then drowns them. After the killing of the young woman Dany, Berenger leaves the radiant city and finally confronts the giggling Killer.

**Exit the King**
A 1962 Berenger-cycle play about the dying King Berenger I, who is more than 400 years old and whose kingdom is collapsing around him. His first wife Queen Marguerite insists he accept death, while his second wife Queen Marie begs him to live, and the Doctor also announces his end.

**Jack, or the Submission**
A play in which Jack's family pressures him into marriage. He rejects a bride with two noses and accepts Roberta II, who has three noses, after she proposes that the word "cat" be used for every concept. Its 1951 sequel is The Future Is in Eggs.

**Victims of Duty**
A 1953 play in which a Detective questions Choubert about a man named Mallot and forces him to eat stale bread to "plug the gaps" in his memory.
